Edge cases to test:

  • All letters distinct → parts of size 1.
  • One letter at both ends → a single part.
  • A single character.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space (26 letters).

Medium 1288. Remove Covered Intervals Google Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Remove every interval that is covered by another (c ≤ a and b ≤ d). Return how many remain.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: intervals = [[1,4],[3,6],[2,8]]
Output: 2
Explanation: Interval [3,6] is covered by [2,8], therefore it is removed.
Example 2
Input: intervals = [[1,4],[2,3]]
Output: 1

Constraints: 1 ≤ intervals.length ≤ 1000 · intervals[i].length == 2 · 0 ≤ li < ri ≤ 10⁵ · All the given intervals are unique.

Hint 1

Sort by start. What must be true about an earlier interval that covers the current one?

Hint 2

Track the maximum end seen; break ties in start by putting longer intervals first.

From brute force to the pattern: Comparing every pair is O(n²). After sorting, one running maximum decides coverage for each interval: O(n log n).

Spot it: Interval relationships → sort by start; then a covering interval always comes before the intervals it covers.

Why not another pattern? Checking every pair is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. Sort by start ascending and, for equal starts, by end descending (the longest first).
  2. Scan, keeping max_end. An interval with end ≤ max_end is covered; otherwise it survives and updates max_end.
class Solution:
    def removeCoveredIntervals(self, intervals: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        intervals = sorted(intervals, key=lambda iv: (iv[0], -iv[1]))  # longest first on equal starts
        remaining = 0
        max_end = 0
        for start, end in intervals:
            if end > max_end:
                remaining = remaining + 1  # not covered by anything before it
                max_end = end
            # else: an earlier interval starts no later and ends no earlier: covered
        return remaining

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. After sorting, every earlier interval starts at or before the current one.
  2. So the current interval is covered exactly when some earlier interval ends at or after it: end <= max_end.
  3. Sorting equal starts by descending end makes the longer interval come first, so it correctly covers the shorter ones.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Identical intervals (one covers the other).
  • Equal starts with different ends.
  • No interval covers another.

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space for the sorted copy.

Hard 715. Range Module Google Array

Problem: Track half-open ranges [left, right): addRange covers a range, removeRange uncovers it, and queryRange asks whether every number in a range is currently covered.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: ["RangeModule", "addRange", "removeRange", "queryRange", "queryRange", "queryRange"] [[], [10, 20], [14, 16], [10, 14], [13, 15], [16, 17]]
Output: [null, null, null, true, false, true]
Explanation: RangeModule rangeModule = new RangeModule(); rangeModule.addRange(10, 20); rangeModule.removeRange(14, 16); rangeModule.queryRange(10, 14); // return True,(Every number in [10, 14) is being tracked) rangeModule.queryRange(13, 15); // return False,(Numbers like 14, 14.03, 14.17 in [13, 15) are not being tracked) rangeModule.queryRange(16, 17); // return True, (The number 16 in [16, 17) is still being tracked, despite the remove operation)

Constraints: 1 ≤ left < right ≤ 10⁹ · At most 10⁴ calls will be made to addRange, queryRange, and removeRange.

Hint 1

Store the covered numbers as a sorted list of disjoint intervals.

Hint 2

Adding merges overlapping intervals; removing splits them; a query only needs the interval that starts at or before left.

From brute force to the pattern: Marking every integer is impossible for ranges up to 10⁹. Keeping disjoint intervals means each operation only touches the intervals that overlap the given range.

Spot it: A set of numbers stored as disjoint, sorted intervals: adding merges overlapping intervals, removing splits them, and querying finds the one interval that could contain the range. That's interval merging plus binary search.

Why not another pattern? A boolean array over all numbers is impossible (up to 10⁹). A segment tree with lazy propagation works but is far more code.

Approach:

  1. Store a sorted list of disjoint intervals.
  2. addRange: drop every interval that overlaps or touches [left, right), extend the new range to cover them, insert it.
  3. removeRange: drop overlapping intervals, but keep their parts sticking out on the left or right.
  4. queryRange: binary-search the last interval starting at or before left; covered if it ends at or after right.
from bisect import bisect_right

class RangeModule:
    def __init__(self):
        self.intervals = []  # sorted, disjoint [start, end) pairs

    def addRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> None:
        kept = []
        for s, e in self.intervals:
            if e < left or s > right:
                kept.append([s, e])  # no overlap and not touching: keep as is
            else:
                left = min(left, s)  # merge it into the new range
                right = max(right, e)
        kept.append([left, right])
        kept.sort()
        self.intervals = kept

    def queryRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> bool:
        starts = [s for s, _ in self.intervals]
        i = bisect_right(starts, left) - 1  # last interval starting at or before left
        return i >= 0 and self.intervals[i][1] >= right

    def removeRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> None:
        kept = []
        for s, e in self.intervals:
            if e <= left or s >= right:
                kept.append([s, e])  # untouched
            else:
                if s < left:
                    kept.append([s, left])  # the part sticking out on the left
                if e > right:
                    kept.append([right, e])  # the part sticking out on the right
        self.intervals = kept

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Intervals are half-open, so [10, 14) and [14, 20) touch; addRange merges touching intervals too (e < left is the strict test).
  2. addRange grows [left, right) to swallow every overlapping interval, then inserts it and re-sorts.
  3. queryRange: only the interval with the largest start ≤ left can contain left; the range is covered if that interval also reaches right.
  4. removeRange keeps the parts of each overlapping interval that lie outside [left, right).

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Adding a range that touches an existing one (merge them).
  • Removing from the middle of an interval (it splits in two).
  • Querying an empty module → False.

Complexity: O(n log n) per addRange, O(n) per removeRange, O(n) per queryRange here (the list of starts is rebuilt; a sorted container makes these O(log n) amortised).

Medium 436. Find Right Interval Amazon Array

Problem: For each interval, return the index of the interval with the smallest start ≥ its end (or −1).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: intervals = [[1,2]]
Output: [-1]
Explanation: There is only one interval in the collection, so it outputs -1.
Example 2
Input: intervals = [[3,4],[2,3],[1,2]]
Output: [-1,0,1]
Explanation: There is no right interval for [3,4]. The right interval for [2,3] is [3,4] since start0 = 3 is the smallest start that is >= end1 = 3. The right interval for [1,2] is [2,3] since start1 = 2 is the smallest start that is >= end2 = 2.

Constraints: 1 ≤ intervals.length ≤ 2 * 10⁴ · intervals[i].length == 2 · -10⁶ ≤ starti ≤ endi ≤ 10⁶ · The start point of each interval is unique.

Hint 1

For each end, you need the smallest start that is at least that end.

Hint 2

Sort the starts and binary-search.

From brute force to the pattern: All pairs: O(n²); sort + binary search: O(n log n).

Spot it: An intervals question answered by sorting starts and binary search: for each end, find the first start at or after it.

Why not another pattern? Checking all pairs is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. starts = sorted((start, index)).
  2. For each interval: bisect_left(starts, (end, −1)); return that index or −1.
from bisect import bisect_left

class Solution:
    def findRightInterval(self, intervals: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        starts = sorted((s, i) for i, (s, _) in enumerate(intervals))
        result = []
        for _, end in intervals:
            j = bisect_left(starts, (end, -1))  # first start >= end
            result.append(starts[j][1] if j < len(starts) else -1)
        return result

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Starts are unique, so (end, −1) sorts before any (end, i), finding a start equal to end too.
  2. An interval can be its own right interval when start == end.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Single interval.
  • start == end (itself).
  • No right interval → −1.

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 646. Maximum Length of Pair Chain Cisco Array

Problem: A pair [c, d] can follow [a, b] if b < c. Return the longest chain (pairs in any order).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: pairs = [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]]
Output: 2
Explanation: The longest chain is [1,2] -> [3,4].
Example 2
Input: pairs = [[1,2],[7,8],[4,5]]
Output: 3
Explanation: The longest chain is [1,2] -> [4,5] -> [7,8].

Constraints: n == pairs.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000 · -1000 ≤ lefti < righti ≤ 1000

Hint 1

Which known interval problem is this?

Hint 2

Sort by end and pick greedily.

From brute force to the pattern: LIS DP is O(n²); the greedy is O(n log n).

Spot it: It's interval scheduling: choose as many non-overlapping intervals as possible → sort by end and take greedily (like Non-overlapping Intervals).

Why not another pattern? The LIS-style DP is O(n²); the greedy is O(n log n).

Approach:

  1. Sort by the second element.
  2. Take a pair if its start is greater than the last taken end.
class Solution:
    def findLongestChain(self, pairs: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        chain = 0
        end = float("-inf")
        for a, b in sorted(pairs, key=lambda p: p[1]):  # earliest end first
            if a > end:
                chain += 1  # it fits after the last chosen pair
                end = b
        return chain

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Choosing the pair that ends earliest leaves the most room for the rest (exchange argument).
  2. Strict > because the chain needs b < c.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Touching pairs (b == c) can't chain.
  • Nested pairs.
  • One pair.

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.

Medium 2021. Brightest Position on Street Microsoft ArrayHash Map

Problem: Lamps light [position − range, position + range]. Return the smallest position with the most lamps lighting it.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ (Premium)

Example 1
Input: lights = [[-3,2],[1,2],[3,3]]
Output: -1
Explanation: Lamps cover [−5, −1], [−1, 3] and [0, 6]. Brightness 2 is the maximum (at −1 and at 0..3); −1 is the smallest such position.
Example 2
Input: lights = [[1,0],[0,1]]
Output: 1
Explanation: Position 1 is lit by both lamps.
Example 3
Input: lights = [[1,2]]
Output: -1
Explanation: Every position in [−1, 3] has brightness 1; −1 is the smallest.

Constraints: 1 ≤ lights.length ≤ 10⁵ · lights[i].length == 2 · -10⁸ ≤ positioni ≤ 10⁸ · 0 ≤ rangei ≤ 10⁸

Hint 1

Brightness changes only at interval ends.

Hint 2

Use a difference map and sweep the sorted points.

From brute force to the pattern: Checking every candidate against every lamp is O(n²); the sweep is O(n log n).

Spot it: Overlapping intervals → a sweep line over a difference map: +1 where a lamp starts, −1 just after it ends; scan the sorted points.

Why not another pattern? Checking each candidate position against every lamp is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. delta[p − r] += 1, delta[p + r + 1] −= 1.
  2. Sweep sorted keys with a running sum; keep the first position with the maximum.
from collections import Counter

class Solution:
    def brightestPosition(self, lights: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        delta = Counter()
        for p, r in lights:
            delta[p - r] += 1  # light starts here
            delta[p + r + 1] -= 1  # and stops after p + r
        best_pos, best = None, -1
        current = 0
        for x in sorted(delta):
            current += delta[x]
            if current > best:
                best, best_pos = current, x  # first (smallest) position with this brightness
        return best_pos

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Brightness only changes at the stored points, so the maximum is reached at one of them.
  2. Strict > keeps the smallest position on ties.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Range 0 (a single point).
  • Ties (smallest position).
  • Negative positions.

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
